title: settle: 'already merged' is a containment question, and containment survives a revert
description:
From the qeu final review (gcx), wave 11 review pass.

settle.go's guard refuses to release a durably rejected attempt whose work is
already merged, because releasing it would dispatch a fresh attempt from a base
that already carries the work — a worker with nothing to do, whose empty branch
is refused, forever. That guard is right for the case it was written for: a GATE
failure, where the merge landed and the repair is the tree.

It asks the wrong question after a REVERT. attemptIsMerged is a containment
question (git merge-base --is-ancestor), and containment survives a revert. An
operator who reverts a bad merged attempt on the integration branch can never
release it: the commit is still an ancestor, so the guard still says "already
merged" and the refusal's premise ("there would be nothing for it to do") is
false — there is now exactly the work to do again.

Worse, without a release the tick does not simply stall: disposition sees a
rejected tick whose remote work IS integrated and takes the adopt path, so the
next run re-gates the REVERTED tree, passes, and closes the tick over work that
is no longer there.

Two things to decide, which is why this is a tick and not a patch:

1. What the right question is. "Is the commit contained" is cheap and wrong
   after a revert. "Is the WORK present" needs a definition — the attempt's
   boundary diff still applying, a tree comparison, or an explicit operator
   statement. Containment plus an operator override may be the honest answer,
   since only a person knows a revert was deliberate.

2. Where the override lives. `ticfac settle <epic> <tick> <attempt> --release
   "<who>"` has no escape today, and adding one must not become a way to waive
   Appendix A #6 (a live attempt is cancelled, never released). Whatever is
   added should be recordable as a decision on origin, the way every other
   settlement is, so the reason a person overrode it outlives them.

Current state: the refusal message names the revert case explicitly and points
here, so an operator who hits it is told what is happening rather than left with
a false premise. That is a signpost, not a fix.
acceptance_criteria: An operator can release a rejected attempt whose merged work was reverted, or is told precisely why they cannot and what to do instead; the chosen answer is recorded as a decision on origin; Appendix A #6 is not waivable by the new path; a test covers the revert case end to end.
